questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man who grew up on a pig farm in rural Mexico and moved to New Jersey 4 years ago is brought to the emergency department after a seizure. He has had intermittent headaches for months. MRI of the brain shows several small viable cysts in the brain parenchyma with mild surrounding edema. Serology for the suspected tapeworm is positive. He is started on an antiseizure medication.

Which additional regimen is most appropriate?
choices: Praziquantel alone as a single dose
Ivermectin with doxycycline
Corticosteroids and albendazole
Triclabendazole alone
Metronidazole with paromomycin

explain.html:
Seizures and parenchymal brain cysts in a man raised on a pig farm in an endemic area, with positive serology, is neurocysticercosis. The two most common presentations are seizures and raised intracranial pressure; diagnosis is imaging, serology, and sometimes biopsy.

Treatment is complicated, but the slides list steroids plus albendazole. Killing the cysts provokes inflammation and edema around them, which the steroids blunt. A single dose of praziquantel is the treatment for intestinal taeniasis, not cysts in the brain.
why: Single-dose praziquantel treats the adult tapeworm in the intestine (taeniasis).
Ivermectin with doxycycline is the approach for Onchocerca.
Triclabendazole treats Fasciola.
Metronidazole with paromomycin treats amebiasis.
explain.takeaway: Neurocysticercosis is diagnosed by imaging and serology and treated with steroids plus albendazole.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 48-year-old man who grew up herding sheep in the Middle East with the help of several dogs is brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle crash with blunt trauma to the right upper abdomen. Within minutes he develops diffuse hives, lip swelling, wheezing, and hypotension. He has received no medications or contrast. CT of the abdomen shows a large cyst in the right lobe of the liver with smaller daughter cysts along its inner wall and fluid around the liver.

Which of the following best explains his acute deterioration?
choices: Release of cyst fluid causing a systemic allergic reaction
Bacterial superinfection of the cyst with septic shock
Rupture of an amebic liver abscess into the peritoneum
Hemorrhage into the peritoneum from a cholangiocarcinoma at the hilum
Disseminated larvae carrying enteric bacteria into blood

explain.html:
A large liver cyst with daughter cysts in someone raised around sheep and dogs is a hydatid cyst of Echinococcus granulosus. Dogs pass eggs in feces, sheep (or humans, as incidental hosts) ingest them, and larvae travel through the blood to the liver or lung, where the cyst slowly grows and is usually asymptomatic until it is large.

Trauma can rupture the cyst. The released cyst fluid is highly antigenic and triggers an allergic reaction that can progress to anaphylaxis, which is exactly what happened here before any drug was given.
why: Septic shock would not produce hives, lip swelling, and wheezing within minutes.
An amebic abscess has no daughter cysts and its rupture is not an allergic event.
Cholangiocarcinoma is linked to liver flukes and does not cause anaphylaxis.
Larvae carrying enteric bacteria into the blood describes Strongyloides hyperinfection.
explain.takeaway: Trauma or rupture of an Echinococcus hydatid cyst releases antigenic fluid that can cause anaphylaxis.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 6-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because she has been scratching her bottom at night and waking up crying for 2 weeks. Her younger brother has started doing the same. She attends a full-day kindergarten. Examination of the perianal skin shows excoriations. Stool ova and parasite examination sent by another clinic last week was negative.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Repeat stool ova and parasite examination on three separate days
Serum antibody testing for the suspected nematode
Clear adhesive tape applied to the perianal skin on waking
Blood smear collected at midnight
Biopsy of the excoriated perianal skin

explain.html:
Nocturnal perianal itching in a young child, spreading within the household, is pinworm (Enterobius vermicularis), the most common helminth in the United States. Adults live in the cecum, and females exit the anus at night to lay eggs on the perianal skin, which causes the itching.

Because eggs are laid on the skin and not in the stool, O&P is not helpful. The test is the scotch tape test, done in the morning or a few hours after sleep, which picks up transparent eggs flattened on one side. Treatment is albendazole, a single dose repeated 2 weeks later, with hot-water laundering for the household.
why: Stool O&P misses pinworm because eggs are deposited on the perianal skin.
Serology is not the test for pinworm.
A midnight blood smear finds Wuchereria or Brugia microfilariae.
Biopsy is invasive and unnecessary; the eggs are on the skin surface.
explain.takeaway: Pinworm causes nocturnal perianal itching; diagnose with the scotch tape test (not stool O&P) and treat with albendazole, repeated in 2 weeks.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 5-year-old girl in a tropical village with poor sanitation is brought to a clinic with chronic diarrhea streaked with blood, abdominal pain, and weight loss. While straining she develops a protrusion of pink, worm-studded rectal mucosa through the anus. Stool microscopy shows barrel-shaped eggs with a plug at each end.

Where do the adult worms causing this condition live?
choices: Jejunum, attached by a scolex
Lymphatic vessels of the pelvis and legs
Bile ducts of the liver
Large intestine, cecum, and appendix
Pulmonary alveoli and bronchi

explain.html:
Bloody diarrhea, weight loss, and rectal prolapse in a child, with eggs that have plugged ends, identify the whipworm, Trichuris trichiura. It is acquired by eating food, water, or soil contaminated with feces containing eggs.

The adults (3 to 5 cm) live in the large intestine, cecum, and appendix, where heavy infection irritates the mucosa and leads to rectal prolapse. Diagnosis is stool O&P and treatment is albendazole plus avoiding contaminated food and water.
why: A scolex attaching to the small intestine describes the tapeworms.
Lymphatics house Wuchereria and Brugia.
Bile ducts house liver flukes such as Clonorchis.
Alveoli hold migrating larvae of Ascaris, hookworm, and Strongyloides, not adult whipworms.
explain.takeaway: Whipworm (Trichuris) lives in the large intestine and cecum, has eggs with plugged ends, and can cause rectal prolapse in children.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old woman comes to the clinic 1 week after returning from a beach vacation in the Caribbean, where she walked barefoot on the sand every day. She has an intensely itchy, raised, red, serpiginous track on the sole of her right foot that she says has moved a few centimeters each day. She feels otherwise well and has no cough, diarrhea, or anemia.

Which of the following best describes this condition?
choices: Dog or cat hookworm larvae that cannot complete their cycle in humans
Human hookworm larvae that will mature into adults in the gut
Strongyloides larvae autoinfecting through the perianal skin
Filarial adult worms migrating through subcutaneous connective tissue
Schistosome cercariae causing a delayed egg granuloma

explain.html:
A moving, itchy, serpiginous track on the foot after walking barefoot on a beach is cutaneous larva migrans, usually caused by dog or cat hookworm larvae (Ancylostoma species) that penetrate human skin.

Humans are not their natural host, so the larvae wander in the skin and die within about 5 to 6 weeks without reaching the lungs or gut. The lesion appears 1 to 5 days after penetration and leaves no long-term effects, which is why she has no cough, diarrhea, or anemia.
why: Human hookworms (Necator, A. duodenale) go on to the lungs and gut and cause anemia, which she does not have.
Strongyloides autoinfection causes larva currens, a fast-moving perianal or trunk rash in chronic infection, not a foot track after one beach trip.
Subcutaneous migrating adult worms describe Loa loa.
Cercariae cause schistosomiasis, whose disease comes from eggs in viscera.
explain.takeaway: Cutaneous larva migrans is a self-limited, migrating skin track from dog or cat hookworm larvae that cannot mature in humans.
explain.topic: Cutaneous larva migrans: humans as dead-end hosts
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman who emigrated from a tropical country 20 years ago is being evaluated before starting a biologic agent for rheumatoid arthritis. She reports occasional epigastric discomfort and recurring, rapidly moving, itchy linear streaks across her lower trunk. Her peripheral eosinophil count is mildly elevated. A single stool ova and parasite examination is negative. She is also found to be positive for human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1).

Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?
choices: No action is needed, because the stool examination was negative
Praziquantel, with a stool recheck in 6 weeks
Albendazole single dose, repeated after 2 weeks
Serology, and treatment with ivermectin before the biologic
Diethylcarbamazine after a daytime blood smear

explain.html:
Larva currens (recurrent, fast-moving itchy linear streaks), vague GI symptoms, and mild eosinophilia years after leaving the tropics suggest chronic Strongyloides, which persists for decades through autoinfection. HTLV-1 and the planned biologic are both risk factors for hyperinfection and dissemination.

Stool O&P has poor sensitivity (three samples are needed), so one negative exam does not exclude it. Serology is the better test, and the treatment is ivermectin, given before immunosuppression to prevent a fatal disseminated infection.
why: A single stool exam is insensitive for Strongyloides, and missing it before a biologic risks dissemination.
Praziquantel treats flukes and tapeworms, not Strongyloides.
Albendazole repeated at 2 weeks is the pinworm regimen.
Diethylcarbamazine after a daytime smear is the approach to Loa loa.
explain.takeaway: Chronic Strongyloides is best diagnosed by serology (stool O&P is insensitive) and treated with ivermectin, especially before steroids, biologics, or with HTLV-1.
explain.topic: Strongyloides: diagnosis and treatment of chronic infection
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man living in Hawaii is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of severe headache, neck stiffness, fever, and burning paresthesias in his legs. Five days earlier he ate a salad made from lettuce from his backyard garden, where slugs and snails are common. Laboratory studies show:

Peripheral eosinophils: 14% (1 to 4)
CSF nucleated cells: 380/microL (0 to 5)
CSF eosinophils: 18% (0)
CSF protein: 58 mg/dL (15 to 45)
CSF glucose: 60 mg/dL (40 to 70)

Which of the following is the most likely cause?
choices: Naegleria fowleri
Angiostrongylus cantonensis
Taenia solium
Toxocara canis
Trichinella spiralis

explain.html:
More than 10% eosinophils in the cerebrospinal fluid defines eosinophilic meningitis. Exposure to snails or slugs on garden vegetables in Hawaii points to Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the rat lungworm, which is found in Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, Hawaii, and the southern United States.

Humans are accidental hosts: ingested larvae travel to the CNS, get stuck, die, and provoke eosinophilic inflammation. Most cases are self-limited, and all treatment is supportive. The leading causes of eosinophilic meningitis are Angiostrongylus and Baylisascaris, ahead of Toxocara.
why: Naegleria causes fulminant meningoencephalitis after warm freshwater swimming, without CSF eosinophilia.
Taenia solium causes neurocysticercosis with seizures and brain cysts.
Toxocara is a less common cause and fits a young child with pica and puppies.
Trichinella causes myalgia and periorbital edema after eating wild-game meat.
explain.takeaway: Eosinophilic meningitis after eating produce contaminated by snails or slugs (Hawaii, Caribbean, southern US) is Angiostrongylus; treatment is supportive.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 7-year-old girl is brought to the ophthalmologist because her teacher noticed she could not see the board with her right eye. Her parents report no fever or other illness. She plays daily in a sandbox shared with neighborhood cats and dogs. Examination shows decreased vision in the right eye only, with a whitish mass on the retina and surrounding chorioretinitis. The left eye is normal. The peripheral eosinophil count is normal. A pediatric oncologist is consulted because of concern for a retinal tumor.

Which of the following is the most likely cause?
choices: Larvae of a dog or cat roundworm lodged in the eye
Microfilariae of a black fly-borne worm in the eye
An adult worm migrating beneath the conjunctiva
Free-living amebae infecting the cornea
Tapeworm cysts lodged in the vitreous after eating pork

explain.html:
Unilateral loss of vision with a retinal mass and chorioretinitis in a school-age child who plays in soil or sand contaminated by dogs and cats is ocular toxocariasis (ocular larva migrans), which mostly affects children 5 to 10 years old. A single larva penetrates one eye, dies, and provokes inflammation.

It can be misdiagnosed as retinoblastoma, and there is often no systemic involvement, so a normal eosinophil count does not exclude it. Treatment focuses on minimizing damage to the eye; albendazole is the antiparasitic.
why: Black fly-borne Onchocerca causes river blindness in adults living near rivers in endemic areas, with skin findings.
A worm migrating under the conjunctiva is Loa loa in an adult from Central Africa.
Free-living amebae infect the cornea in contact lens wearers (Acanthamoeba keratitis).
Cysticerci of T. solium come from ingesting eggs, not pork, and do not fit this pet exposure.
explain.takeaway: Ocular toxocariasis, a unilateral retinal lesion in a child 5 to 10 years old exposed to dog or cat feces, can be mistaken for retinoblastoma and often lacks systemic signs.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 36-year-old woman who was born in New York City, has never traveled outside the United States, and keeps a strict vegetarian diet is brought to the emergency department after a first generalized seizure. CT of the head shows two small ring-enhancing cystic lesions in the cerebral cortex, and serology confirms a tapeworm infection of the brain. Her live-in housekeeper, who recently arrived from a rural pig-raising region of Central America, is later found to have tapeworm segments in her stool.

Which of the following best explains how this patient became infected?
choices: She ate undercooked pork containing larval cysts
She was bitten by a fly carrying infective larvae
Larvae penetrated her skin from contaminated soil
She ingested eggs shed in the housekeeper's feces
She ate raw freshwater fish containing larvae

explain.html:
Ring-enhancing brain cysts with seizures are neurocysticercosis (NCC) from Taenia solium, the pork tapeworm. The route decides the disease: eating pork that contains cysticerci leaves an adult tapeworm in the intestine (taeniasis), while ingesting the eggs lets larvae travel to muscle, eyes, and brain and form cysticerci there.

So NCC does not require eating pork. A household contact carrying the adult tapeworm sheds eggs in feces, and fecal contamination of food or hands transmits them; household contacts have about a 3-fold higher risk. The housekeeper with taeniasis is the source.
why: Eating pork with cysticerci causes intestinal taeniasis, not brain cysts, and she does not eat meat.
Fly bites transmit filarial worms such as Loa loa and Onchocerca.
Skin penetration from soil is the route of hookworm and Strongyloides.
Raw fish transmits the fish tapeworm and liver flukes, not cysticercosis.
explain.takeaway: Neurocysticercosis comes from ingesting T. solium eggs (fecal-oral, often from a household tapeworm carrier); eating larvae in pork causes only intestinal taeniasis.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 61-year-old man from northern Finland comes to the clinic with fatigue, shortness of breath on exertion, and tingling in both feet. He regularly eats raw and lightly salted fish caught in cold local lakes. Hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL (13.5 to 17.5) with a mean corpuscular volume of 118 fL (80 to 100), and a peripheral smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. Stool ova and parasite examination shows operculated eggs, and he recalls passing long flat segments of worm.

Which of the following best explains his anemia?
choices: Adult worms ingest red blood cells in the small intestine
Macrophages in the spleen are filled with parasite forms
Larvae invade the bone marrow and replace normal cells
Chronic blood loss from colonic ulcers causes iron deficiency
The tapeworm competes for and absorbs dietary vitamin B12

explain.html:
Eating raw fish from cold lakes of Northern Europe with passage of flat worm segments and eggs in stool identifies Diphyllobothrium latum, the fish tapeworm. It is the longest of the intestinal tapeworms (about 10 meters) and can live 25 years.

The worm takes up vitamin B12 in the gut, and about 40% of patients develop megaloblastic anemia, which fits the high MCV, hypersegmented neutrophils, and neuropathy. Like the other intestinal tapeworms it is diagnosed by eggs on stool O&P and treated with praziquantel.
why: Red cell ingestion in the small intestine is how hookworms cause iron deficiency (microcytic) anemia.
Parasite-filled splenic macrophages describe visceral leishmaniasis.
Tapeworm larvae do not replace the bone marrow.
Colonic blood loss would give a microcytic picture and fits Trichuris or amebiasis, not this macrocytosis.
explain.takeaway: The fish tapeworm Diphyllobothrium latum (raw fish from cold lakes) causes megaloblastic anemia from vitamin B12 deficiency.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 40-year-old woman from a sheep-raising region of South America comes to the clinic with 6 months of dull right upper quadrant fullness. Ultrasound shows a 12-cm cyst in the liver containing multiple smaller internal cysts. Serology is positive for the suspected cestode. A student on the team orders three stool ova and parasite examinations, and all are negative.

Which of the following best explains the negative stool studies?
choices: Eggs are shed only at night onto the perianal skin
Too few eggs are shed, so many more samples are needed
Humans carry only the larval cyst, never an egg-laying adult
Eggs are destroyed by gastric acid before reaching stool
Eggs are passed in urine rather than in the feces

explain.html:
A large liver cyst with internal daughter cysts in a person from a sheep-raising area, with positive serology, is hydatid disease from Echinococcus. The adult tapeworm lives in the small intestine of dogs, the definitive host; humans are incidental hosts that ingest eggs and develop only the larval hydatid cyst in liver or lung.

Because no adult worm lives in the human gut, no eggs appear in stool, and O&P is not a useful test. Diagnosis is imaging (ultrasound, CT) plus serology, and treatment depends on the cyst stage: resection if curative, and albendazole.
why: Nocturnal perianal egg laying describes the pinworm.
More samples help for Strongyloides, but no number of stool samples finds Echinococcus eggs in humans.
Gastric acid is not the reason; there is simply no adult worm in the human intestine.
Eggs in urine describe urinary schistosomiasis.
explain.takeaway: Humans are incidental hosts of Echinococcus carrying only the hydatid cyst, so stool O&P is negative; diagnose by imaging and serology.
explain.topic: Echinococcus: why stool testing fails and humans are dead-end hosts
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 4-year-old boy in a rural area with poor sanitation is brought to the clinic with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and abdominal distension. His mother noticed a large, pale, smooth worm about 20 cm long in his stool. Two months ago he had a week of dry cough and wheezing that resolved without treatment; a chest x-ray at that time showed transient patchy infiltrates, and the eosinophil count was elevated.

Which of the following best explains the earlier respiratory illness?
choices: Larvae penetrated the skin of his feet and reached the lungs
Antibodies to the adult worm cross-reacted with lung tissue
Eggs were inhaled in dust and hatched within the alveoli
Adult worms migrated up the esophagus into the trachea
Larvae hatched in the gut traveled via the liver to the lungs

explain.html:
A 15 to 30 cm roundworm passed in stool, with obstruction in a heavily infected child, is Ascaris lumbricoides, a soil-transmitted helminth acquired by swallowing eggs from contaminated soil or vegetation.

The ingested eggs hatch into larvae in the gut, which cross the mucosa, travel in the blood to the liver, then to the lungs, ascend the bronchi, and are swallowed to mature in the intestine (GUT, LIVER, LUNGS, GUT). Passage through the lungs causes Loeffler syndrome, an eosinophilic pneumonitis with wheeze, dry cough, and transient infiltrates. Diagnosis is mammillated eggs on stool O&P, and treatment is albendazole.
why: Skin penetration followed by lung passage is the route of hookworm and Strongyloides, not Ascaris.
Loeffler syndrome reflects migrating larvae and eosinophils, not cross-reacting antibodies.
Ascaris eggs are swallowed, not inhaled.
Adults live in the intestine; the lung phase is larval.
explain.takeaway: Ascaris larvae follow GUT, LIVER, LUNGS, GUT; their lung passage causes Loeffler syndrome (eosinophilic pneumonitis with transient infiltrates).
explain.topic: Ascaris: larval migration through the lungs
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 12-year-old boy from a rural community with outdoor latrines and no indoor plumbing is brought to the clinic because of fatigue, poor school performance, and pallor. He usually goes barefoot. He has had no blood in his stool. Laboratory studies show:

Hemoglobin: 8.2 g/dL (12 to 16)
Mean corpuscular volume: 66 fL (80 to 100)
Ferritin: 5 ng/mL (15 to 200)
Serum albumin: 3.0 g/dL (3.5 to 5.5)
Eosinophils: 9% (1 to 4)

Stool microscopy shows thin-shelled oval eggs.

Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his anemia?
choices: Vitamin B12 absorbed by a long intestinal tapeworm
Bleeding from flask-shaped ulcers in the colon
Hemolysis of red cells parasitized by protozoa
Marrow suppression caused by circulating microfilariae
Adult worms attached in the small intestine feed on blood

explain.html:
Microcytic iron deficiency anemia with low albumin and eosinophilia in a barefoot child in an area with poor sanitation points to hookworm (Necator americanus or Ancylostoma duodenale). Larvae in soil penetrate the skin, travel to the lungs, are coughed up and swallowed, and mature in the small intestine (SKIN, LUNGS, GUT).

The adults attach to the small intestinal wall and constantly suck blood, producing iron deficiency anemia, and chronic heavy infection adds protein deficiency (low albumin). Diagnosis is eggs in stool, and treatment is albendazole. In the United States, campaigns against hookworm improved school attendance and literacy.
why: B12 uptake by the fish tapeworm causes a macrocytic, not microcytic, anemia.
Flask-shaped ulcers cause bloody diarrhea from amebiasis, which he does not have.
Intraerythrocytic protozoa are not part of this picture, and hemolysis would not deplete ferritin.
Microfilariae circulate in blood but do not suppress the marrow.
explain.takeaway: Hookworm larvae enter through bare skin (SKIN, LUNGS, GUT) and adults in the small intestine feed on blood, causing iron deficiency anemia and protein deficiency.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old man who worked as a coal miner in Appalachia is started on high-dose prednisone for a flare of an autoimmune disease. For years he has had intermittent epigastric pain, alternating diarrhea and constipation, and an itchy, linear rash on his buttocks that comes and goes. Three weeks after starting prednisone he develops fever, wheezing, hemoptysis, and abdominal pain, then becomes confused. Blood cultures grow Escherichia coli, and cerebrospinal fluid shows gram-negative rods.

Which of the following best explains the bacteremia and meningitis?
choices: Corticosteroids suppressed neutrophil production
Ruptured hydatid cyst seeded the blood with bacteria
Larvae penetrating the bowel wall carried enteric bacteria
Adult worms obstructed and perforated the intestine
Microfilariae in the blood triggered sepsis at night

explain.html:
Years of mild GI symptoms with recurrent linear perianal streaks (larva currens) in a coal miner from Appalachia is chronic Strongyloides stercoralis. Its unique autoinfection cycle lets larvae penetrate the gut mucosa or perianal skin and keeps the infection going for decades.

When high-dose corticosteroids are started, larval migration increases enormously (hyperinfection). Larvae penetrating the bowel wall carry gut bacteria with them, causing gram-negative rod bacteremia and meningitis in disseminated strongyloidiasis, which is fatal in 50 to 90%. Screening and treating with ivermectin before immunosuppression is the prevention.
why: Steroids raise neutrophil counts, and this pattern of enteric gram-negative rods after larva currens points to the worm.
Hydatid cyst rupture causes anaphylaxis, not gram-negative meningitis.
Intestinal obstruction from adult worms is an Ascaris complication in children.
Nocturnal microfilariae belong to lymphatic filariasis and do not cause bacteremia.
explain.takeaway: In chronic Strongyloides, corticosteroids trigger hyperinfection and dissemination; larvae crossing the bowel carry gram-negative rods into the blood and meninges.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with 3 weeks of intermittent fever, cough with wheezing, and a decreased appetite. His parents have seen him eating dirt in the backyard, where the family's new puppies play. The liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Leukocyte count is 24,000/microL (4,500 to 11,000) with 52% eosinophils (1 to 4). Stool ova and parasite examination is negative.

Which of the following is the best test to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Serum ELISA for antibodies to the larvae
Three more stool ova and parasite examinations
Scotch tape test of the perianal skin
Blood smear drawn at night for microfilariae
Sputum examination for operculated eggs

explain.html:
A young child with pica, puppies in the yard, fever, wheezing, hepatomegaly, and very high eosinophilia has visceral larva migrans from Toxocara canis (or T. cati). Dogs and cats are the definitive hosts; humans are incidental hosts who swallow eggs from soil, and the larvae disseminate, die, and provoke eosinophilic inflammation and granulomas.

The larvae never mature in the human gut, so no eggs are released and stool O&P is not helpful. Diagnosis is serology (ELISA, sensitivity about 70 to 75%) or histology showing granulomas, and treatment is albendazole.
why: Stool exams cannot find Toxocara because no eggs are released in the human gut.
The scotch tape test finds pinworm eggs.
A night smear finds Wuchereria and Brugia microfilariae.
Eggs in sputum suggest Paragonimus.
explain.takeaway: Toxocara (puppies, pica, eosinophilia, hepatomegaly) cannot mature in humans, so stool O&P is negative; diagnosis is by serology.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Three hunters come to the emergency department 10 days after sharing grilled bear meat cooked rare at a hunting camp. All have fever, severe muscle pain and tenderness, and swelling around both eyes; two had abdominal pain and diarrhea during the first week. Laboratory studies in one show eosinophils of 26% (1 to 4) and a markedly elevated creatine kinase.

Which of the following tests would best confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Stool ova and parasite examination
Lumbar puncture to count eosinophils in the CSF
Scotch tape test of the perianal skin
Skin snip biopsy placed in saline
Serum antibody testing or muscle biopsy

explain.html:
Fever, eosinophilia, severe myalgia, and periorbital edema after eating undercooked bear (or pig or cougar) meat is trichinellosis from Trichinella spiralis. Larvae ingested in the meat mature in the gut and their offspring travel to striated muscle and encyst; involvement of the muscles around the eye produces periorbital edema.

The diagnosis is made by serum antibody or muscle biopsy showing the encysted larvae, and treatment is albendazole, with steroids if severe. Cooking meat to an internal temperature of at least 165 F (74 C) kills the parasite.
why: The disease lives in muscle, so stool O&P is not a reliable way to confirm it.
CSF eosinophils point to Angiostrongylus or Baylisascaris, not this myositis picture.
The scotch tape test is for pinworm.
A skin snip in saline is the test for Onchocerca.
explain.takeaway: Trichinella (undercooked bear or pork: fever, myalgia, periorbital edema, eosinophilia) is confirmed by serology or muscle biopsy and treated with albendazole, plus steroids if severe.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old man who lived for several years in the rainforest region of Central Africa comes to the clinic with episodes of painless, nonred swelling of the forearm that last a few days and then move elsewhere. Last week he felt something crawling across his eye, and an ophthalmologist removed a thin worm from under the conjunctiva. A blood smear drawn at noon shows microfilariae at high density. Skin snips for other filariae are negative.

Which of the following is the major concern when choosing treatment?
choices: Diethylcarbamazine in heavy infection can cause brain inflammation
Praziquantel will cause rupture of hydatid cysts
Ivermectin will reverse established lymphedema
Doxycycline cannot kill the adult worms because they lack bacteria
Corticosteroids trigger dissemination of autoinfecting larvae

explain.html:
Migrating painless swellings (Calabar swellings), a worm crossing the eye, and microfilariae in blood drawn during the day identify Loa loa, the African eye worm, transmitted by Chrysops flies in the rainforests of West and Central Africa. Adults move through subcutaneous connective tissue and release microfilariae into the blood during the day.

Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) kills both microfilariae and adults, but with a heavy microfilarial load it carries a risk of brain inflammation after administration, and it should not be used where Onchocerca is endemic. That caution is the key decision here.
why: Hydatid cysts belong to Echinococcus, which this patient does not have.
Antihelminthics do not reverse lymphedema, and lymphedema is a feature of Wuchereria, not Loa loa.
Doxycycline kills Onchocerca adults by targeting Wolbachia; it is not part of the Loa loa regimen on the slides.
Steroid-triggered dissemination is a Strongyloides problem.
explain.takeaway: Loa loa (Chrysops fly, Calabar swellings, eye worm) is diagnosed by a daytime blood smear; DEC treats it but risks brain inflammation with heavy infection.
explain.topic: Loa loa: daytime smear and risk with diethylcarbamazine
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old farmer from a West African village near a fast-flowing river comes to a clinic with years of intense itching that keeps him from working, thickened skin on his legs, and firm, painless nodules over his hips. His vision has gradually worsened. A slit-lamp examination shows inflammation and scarring of the cornea, and a skin snip biopsy placed in saline releases microfilariae. He is treated with ivermectin and doxycycline.

Doxycycline is included in the regimen because it does which of the following?
choices: Paralyzes the microfilariae circulating in the blood at night
Kills endosymbiotic bacteria that adult worms need to survive
Treats bacterial superinfection of the scratched skin
Prevents the brain inflammation caused by ivermectin
Blocks the black fly vector from transmitting larvae

explain.html:
Severe itching, skin nodules, a skin snip that releases microfilariae, and eye inflammation that progresses to blindness in a villager near a fast river is onchocerciasis (river blindness) from Onchocerca volvulus, transmitted by black flies. Adults live in skin nodules and release microfilariae into the skin and eyes.

Ivermectin kills microfilariae and sterilizes the female worms but does not kill the adults. Doxycycline kills the adults indirectly: it eliminates the Wolbachia bacteria that live in the adult worms and are essential to their development, and without Wolbachia the adult worm dies.
why: Onchocerca microfilariae live in the skin, not the night blood, and doxycycline does not target them.
Superinfection is not the reason doxycycline is part of the antiparasitic regimen.
The brain inflammation warning on the slides applies to diethylcarbamazine in heavy Loa loa infection.
Doxycycline does not act on the fly vector.
explain.takeaway: In onchocerciasis, ivermectin kills microfilariae and sterilizes females, while doxycycline kills adult worms by eliminating their Wolbachia endosymbionts.

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man from a coastal region of West Africa where both lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis are common comes to a clinic with progressive, nonpitting swelling of the left leg over several years, with thickened skin. He recalls frequent mosquito bites. A blood smear drawn at 11 PM shows microfilariae, and an antifilarial antibody test is positive.

Which of the following is the most appropriate antiparasitic treatment?
choices: Diethylcarbamazine alone
Albendazole plus ivermectin
Praziquantel alone
Triclabendazole alone
Metronidazole plus paromomycin

explain.html:
Years of leg lymphedema progressing toward elephantiasis, mosquito exposure, and microfilariae in blood drawn at night (nighttime periodicity) identify lymphatic filariasis, 90% caused by Wuchereria bancrofti (with Brugia malayi). Adults live in the lymphatics, and in about 30% of infected people the lymphatics are damaged.

The treatment depends on whether Onchocerca is also present. Without it, DEC is used; where Onchocerca is present, albendazole plus ivermectin is given instead, since DEC should not be used where onchocerciasis is endemic. Antihelminthics will not reverse the existing lymphedema because the lymphatic damage is permanent.
why: DEC is the choice only when Onchocerca is absent, and this region has both.
Praziquantel treats flukes and tapeworms.
Triclabendazole treats Fasciola.
Metronidazole plus paromomycin treats amebiasis.
explain.takeaway: Lymphatic filariasis (mosquito, night blood smear) is treated with DEC if Onchocerca is absent or albendazole plus ivermectin if present; neither reverses lymphedema.
